story.text: One process in Barents Sea & Svalbard and Ross Sea (Antarctica): in each, sea ice cover and air temperature leave their norm in the same months in opposite directions — the same transformation carries one onto the other in every region, although the trends differ (in Barents Sea & Svalbard, sea ice cover falls and air temperature rises; in Ross Sea (Antarctica), sea ice cover rises and air temperature falls).

Opposite trends: sea ice cover is rising in Ross Sea (Antarctica) and falling in Barents Sea & Svalbard. One process can push the same variable in opposite directions in two places — look at the links below to see whether the same months move both.

Opposite trends: air temperature is rising in Barents Sea & Svalbard and falling in Ross Sea (Antarctica). One process can push the same variable in opposite directions in two places — look at the links below to see whether the same months move both.

Sea ice cover — Barents Sea & Svalbard: -3.4 % per decade (95 % range -4.78 to -2.11). Significant falling trend: both tests agree at the 95 % level. Mann-Kendall p = 1.3e-05, t-test p = 0.00015. Eva's dynamics, read year by year: one steady dynamic from 1981 to 2025 (-3.5 per decade): no change of regime stands out from the year-to-year swings. Eva: Since 2011, 79 % of months came out lower than Eva's norm expected from their neighbours (50 % if nothing had changed): the dynamic has left the norm she learned in 1981–2010.

Air temperature — Barents Sea & Svalbard: +0.68 °C per decade (95 % range +0.559 to +0.835). Significant rising trend: both tests agree at the 95 % level. Mann-Kendall p = 3.4e-15, t-test p = 0.00047. Eva's dynamics, read year by year: one steady dynamic from 1981 to 2025 (+0.697 per decade): no change of regime stands out from the year-to-year swings. Eva: Since 2011, 75 % of months came out higher than Eva's norm expected from their neighbours (50 % if nothing had changed): the dynamic has left the norm she learned in 1981–2010.

Air temperature — Ross Sea (Antarctica): -0.56 °C per decade (95 % range -0.772 to -0.344). Significant falling trend: both tests agree at the 95 % level. Mann-Kendall p = 6.9e-05, t-test p = 0.00011. Eva's dynamics, read year by year: one steady dynamic from 1981 to 2025 (-0.563 per decade): no change of regime stands out from the year-to-year swings. Eva: Since 2011, 64 % of months came out lower than Eva's norm expected from their neighbours (50 % if nothing had changed): the dynamic has left the norm she learned in 1981–2010.

Sea ice cover (Barents Sea & Svalbard) and Air temperature (Barents Sea & Svalbard) leave their norm in the same months, in opposite directions: 93 times, where chance at the same moment of the record would give 53 (p = 7e-11; z = 7.0 against the same reading with one of them moved 1 to 5 years, beyond the shared trend and the persistence of each). Model note: both series come from the MERRA-2 reanalysis, not from two independent instruments: confirm it with an independent dataset before calling it a finding.

story.text: Sea ice cover — Ross Sea (Antarctica): +1.2 % per decade (95 % range +0.145 to +2.36). A rising trend that only one test (or only the 90 % level) supports. Mann-Kendall p = 0.019, t-test p = 0.077. With this much natural variability, a trend of this size needs about 59 years of data to stand out (45 so far). Eva's dynamics, read year by year: one steady dynamic from 1981 to 2025 (+1.34 per decade): no change of regime stands out from the year-to-year swings. Eva: Since 2011, 61 % of months came out higher than Eva's norm expected from their neighbours (50 % if nothing had changed): the dynamic has left the norm she learned in 1981–2010.

Sea ice cover (Barents Sea & Svalbard): in 52 of 520 grid cells, the level dropped and then the trend turned downward (chance gives that sequence in as many cells, anywhere, 0.01 of the time or less). A sequence of changes of dynamic, cell by cell; a reanalysis still, to be checked against independent data.

Sea ice cover (Barents Sea & Svalbard): in 52 of 520 grid cells, the trend turned upward and then the level dropped (chance gives that sequence in as many cells, anywhere, 0.01 of the time or less). A sequence of changes of dynamic, cell by cell; a reanalysis still, to be checked against independent data.
